In order to satisfy RIP, it is simplest to make C a random matrix. Two of the most common for this use are the Gaussian matrix or Bernoulli matrix1. A Gaussian matrix is some M×N matrix filled with random values centered at 0 with a standard deviation of 1. The Bernoulli matrix is comprised of 0’s and 1’s, where each cell in the matrix and some probability p (0 < p < 1) of being 1 and probability 1-p of being 0. Both matrices will produce very similar results simply because they both satisfy RIP, but the Gaussian matrix is computationally expensive due to the number of calculations required, especially with high- dimensional data. Thus, in this project, we use a Bernoulli matrix with a probability of 0.1 as the random matrix C. B. Calculations and Algorithms Once the measurement vector y is created via Equation 6, we are able to proceed to reconstruction via minimizing the error in the x vector. We want the vector with the most sparsity, so we ideally should choose to optimize the L0-norm. Though this would be ideal, the L0-norm is non-convex and NP-Hard, meaning it is a combinatorially hard question that cannot be solved in polynomial time with an algorithm9. To circumvent this, we aim to minimize the L1- norm instead which is a convex relaxation of the L0-norm that typically yields the same answer1. Due to its convexity10, there are many algorithms used for L1 minimization, in this project, we use the LASSO regularization algorithm. LASSO is a regression technique that uses the L1-norm’s convex property and its ability to promote sparsity to do L1 regularization in order to achieve the sparsest possible solution. As opposed to typical least squares methods, this algorithm also uses a parameter called the L1 penalty (λ) which optimizes the balance between bias and variance and is found through cross- validation 11. An excess of bias leads to an over-simplified reconstruction which does not capture enough of the true data, while too much variance overfits the reconstruction and creates a far too complex recreation3. As found in Brunton’s textbook ‘Data Driven Science and Engineering’1, taking this variable into account results in the following optimization equation: x = argmin(x’) ||Cx’-y|| + λ||x|| (7) 2 1 This equation translates to finding the optimized x’ vector such that Cx’-y is close to zero and x is as sparse as possible. 5 After the reconstructed signal is calculated, we are able to simply plot the signal without any inverse transformation functions because no domain transfer occurred.
